title: Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks Whether They Work
dek: Australia puts supplements and medicines under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market entry nor tested during production — the impression of ‘good’ was planted by marketing and cross-border policy.
why: The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the back half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garbage, so the information density is uneven.
who: Investors and founders looking at consumer brands, supplements and cross-border e-commerce, plus anyone doing brand marketing or interested in where regulatory arbitrage exists.
skip: 14:35-15:05 has a stretch of transcription garbage that can be skipped without losing the thread.

points.h: Australians taking pills is a tradition, not a climate
points.body: The soil for Australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a sparse population that self-medicates, pharmacists who also diagnose and dispense, natural-therapy industry bodies dating to the 1920s, and health food stores resembling food-as-medicine shops. Stack those four together and Australians take it for granted that you solve health problems without going to hospital. Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathy clinic; only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognise — turning ‘a spoonful of fish oil a day’ into a standardised fish oil capsule.

points.h: The contract manufacturers are the industry's foundation
points.body: Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing of supplements, and by around 2003 it was producing roughly 70% of Australia's vitamins, minerals and herbal products. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, sealing the gelatin shell and oils of soft capsules, powder blend uniformity, liquid stability — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s and 90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended service in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labelling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only has to hand over a concept and the factory can turn it into a product ready to sell.

points.h: Registration means nobody looks before it hits the shelf
points.body: Australia legislated in 1989, putting the TGA in charge of both medicines and supplements, and all products must obtain an AUST number. Most supplements fall into the AUSTL category: only low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA, only low-level health claims, and companies get a number just by applying themselves — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had roughly ten thousand complementary medicines, nearly 98% of them in this registration system. Only prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, which requires the TGA to assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

points.h: It looks strict, but in practice it is loose
points.body: Put the contract manufacturing and regulatory lines together and GMP only guarantees that the factory produces consistently to the standard the brand gives it, and that problems can be traced back to a batch for recall — it is not itself responsible for whether the product works. The TGA side only handles filings and issuing numbers; efficacy is the brand's own claim to make. So the statement that ‘Australia regulates supplements like drugs’ is not wrong in itself, but it is misleading: the method of regulation is the same, the regulatory standard applied to the efficacy part differs enormously. The whole system exercises no effective upfront oversight of whether a product actually works, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and the product's efficacy.

points.h: The marketing was copied from Centrum, not invented
points.body: CEO Radek Sali, who took over in 2008, did not conjure a marketing plan out of thin air. He did industry research and found the best seller among peers was Centrum, and the feedback from retailers was: Centrum doesn't give the channel much margin, but you can't argue with it advertising heavily on TV all year, with good athlete endorsements, so consumers walk into the pharmacy and ask for it by name. Sali wanted to replicate that at Swisse. He started with Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain, buying very short ad slots only during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so a limited budget could still appear at the key moments. But the female-dominated sales channel wasn't impressed; one buyer didn't watch cricket herself and didn't know the athlete. He asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said a dance reality show, and the strategy pivoted to spoken-word spots in entertainment content.

Swisse's bigger promotional push drew on Oprah and Ellen, and signed a three-year deal with the actress Nicole Kidman, extending its reach from Australia to the United States. By 2012 Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, and reached annual revenue of A$183 million, with marketing spend of A$40-50 million a year — said at one point to be the highest marketing spend of any consumer brand in Australia. Its ads didn't stress efficacy or ingredients; they mainly presented a state of being energetic, self-disciplined and good-looking — converting health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse took more than 20% market share in Australian supermarkets and more than 10% in pharmacies.

points.h: The growth engine was found in Chinese pharmacies
points.body: Swisse's expensive push into the US market was not a success, and back home in Australia it found that Swisse sold extremely well in pharmacies in Chinese-populated areas, with some stores selling at ten times the level of an ordinary store — because students and Chinese migrants were buying in bulk to take back to China or resell online, that is, daigou. Two policy shifts came in 2015: in March the Hangzhou cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which took effect that December. The FTA mainly affects ordinary trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average of 20%, and after the agreement it was said at the time that this could fall to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce goes through bonded warehouses, platforms buy in bulk, logistics time and cost drop sharply, and such goods are treated in policy as for personal use, so they don't have to go through the registration and filing process for supplement imports.

points.h: The brand was bought; the impression stayed put
points.body: In September 2015 the Hong Kong-listed company Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full buyout, a deal of about A$1.7 billion, or RMB 8.7 billion. For Swisse the deal carried little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. All those Swisse ads in Hunan TV variety shows now are, in theory, a Chinese supplement company spending the money, but the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their old, vague good impression of Australia to it — a large share of the acquisition's core value sits in brand goodwill.

quotes.text: The GMP system itself is not responsible for the product's efficacy; it can only prove that the contract manufacturer produced to the standard the brand gave it.
The whole system is, in fact, strict in appearance and loose in practice, especially when it comes to the efficacy part.
This looseness means that no part of the system exercises any effective upfront oversight of whether the product actually works.
It doesn't stress efficacy or ingredients; it mainly presents a state of being energetic, self-disciplined and good-looking — turning health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to.
There's no particular barrier in the supplement industry; if everyone doesn't compete on marketing, for now they haven't found the next thing to compete on.
When consumers face something they're unfamiliar with, it's actually very easy for them to string together other familiar and trustworthy concepts to make sense of the unfamiliar thing.

We tend to remember very simple concepts or judgments, so simple that you forget how many layers of logic lie behind them. So the more a business idea looks like common sense, the more it's worth asking one more question: how did it come about, and how did it become so-called common sense?
